title: Is Light a Wave or a Particle?
hook: Light behaves like a wave in some experiments and like a stream of particles in others — and the surprising answer is that it's both.
key_points: Light spreads, interferes, and diffracts like a wave.
It also arrives in discrete packets of energy called photons, like particles.
This wave-particle duality is a core idea of quantum physics.
Which behavior you see depends on the experiment you run.
content_html: For centuries physicists argued over whether light was a wave or a stream of tiny particles. Wave experiments seemed decisive: light spreads around corners, bends through lenses, and produces interference patterns where overlapping beams add up or cancel out — all hallmarks of waves. But other experiments stubbornly showed light arriving in discrete chunks of energy, behaving like particles.
extra_html: The resolution, and one of the founding insights of quantum physics, is that light is both. It travels and spreads like a wave, yet it's delivered and absorbed in indivisible packets called photons. Which face it shows depends on the experiment you set up to look at it — no single classical picture captures the whole story. This wave-particle duality isn't unique to light, either; matter such as electrons turns out to behave the same way. Britannica traces the history of the debate and how duality settled it.

related.title: Reflection & Refraction
related.hook: A straw looks bent in a glass of water — not because the straw bends, but because light does when it changes speed.

related.title: What Makes Quantum Physics Weird
related.hook: In the quantum world energy comes in lumps, particles act like waves, and you can't pin down everything at once — and yet it's our best-tested theory.

related.title: The Photoelectric Effect
related.hook: Shine the wrong color of light on a metal and nothing happens, no matter how bright. Switch to a bluer color and electrons fly off instantly. That puzzle proved light comes in packets.

flashcards.back_html: Light behaves as a wave (spreading, interfering) in some experiments and as a stream of particles — photons — in others. It is genuinely both.

flashcards.prompt: Which behavior of light reveals its wave nature rather than its particle nature?

choices.text: Producing interference patterns where overlapping beams reinforce or cancel
Arriving in discrete, countable packets of energy
Knocking individual electrons off a metal surface

flashcards.explanation_html: Interference and diffraction are wave hallmarks. Arriving in packets (photons) and ejecting single electrons instead reveal light's particle side.
